excerpt: Pandoc can convert between numerous markup and word processing formats, including, but not limited to, various flavors of Markdown, HTML, LaTeX and Word docx.
The input format can be specified using the -f/--from option, the output format using the -t/--to option.
If the input or output format is not specified explicitly, pandoc will attempt to guess it from the extensions of the filenames.
To produce a standalone document (e.g. a valid HTML file including <head> and <body>), use the -s or --standalone flag
If no input-files are specified, input is read from stdin. Output goes to stdout by default.
If multiple input files are given, pandoc will concatenate them all (with blank lines between them) before parsing.
To produce a PDF, specify an output file with a .pdf extension: pandoc test.txt -o test.pdf
When HTML is used as an intermediate format, the output can be styled using --css.
→ via pdflatex, lualatex, xelatex, latexmk, tectonic, wkhtmltopdf, weasyprint, prince, pagedjs-cli, context, or pdfroff.
To debug the PDF creation, it can be useful to look at the intermediate representation: instead of -o test.pdf, use for example -s -o test.tex
Instead of an input file, an absolute URI may be given. In this case pandoc will fetch the content using HTTP
It is possible to supply a custom User-Agent string or other header when requesting a document from a URL
Extensions can be individually enabled or disabled by appending +EXTENSION or -EXTENSION to the format name.
You can also use pandoc --list-input-formats and pandoc --list-output-formats to print lists of supported formats.
Users can also run custom pandoc filters to modify the intermediate AST
custom readers and writers can be written in Lua
Pandoc includes a Haskell library and a standalone command-line program.
pandoc will convert it into a properly formatted citation using any of hundreds of CSL styles ... and add a properly formatted bibliography at the end of the document.
LaTeX math (and even macros) can be used in markdown documents. Several different methods of rendering math in HTML are provided, including MathJax and translation to MathML.
If strict markdown compatibility is desired, all of these extensions can be turned off.
revealjs (reveal.js HTML5 + JavaScript slide show)
→ InDesign ICML
← CSV tables ← TSV tables ← Microsoft Excel spreadsheets
↔︎ Jupyter notebook (ipynb)
There are many ways to customize pandoc to fit your needs, including a template system and a powerful system for writing filters.
chunkedhtml (zip archive of multiple linked HTML files)
a limited online demo, and a WebAssembly-based online demo
Alternatively, you can install pandoc using Homebrew: brew install pandoc
Alternatively, you can install pandoc using Chocolatey: choco install pandoc
The pandoc/latex image also contains the minimal LaTeX installation needed to produce PDFs using pandoc.
Pandoc can be run through GitHub Actions. For some examples, see https://github.com/pandoc/pandoc-action-example.
It is possible to compile pandoc such that the data files pandoc uses are embedded in the binary. The resulting binary can be run from any directory and is completely self-contained.
server: compile in support for running in HTTP server mode when the executable is renamed (or symlinked as) pandoc-server.

Does all academic writing in Pandoc. Compared to LaTeX there is no boilerplate, but full LaTeX equation syntax is still available. If a publisher needs Word, it's one click away. The plain-text sources can go under version control with meaningful diffs.
Their attempts to use Pandoc (possibly an older version) usually butchered the document, because the internal representation wasn't as expressive as the source or target formats.

In 2.2.3.2, Markdown-to-Markdown round trips lose some details: reference-style links become inline links, setext headers become hash headers, and two-space line breaks become trailing backslashes. These are occasional nuisances; documents aren't butchered.
Frustratingly slow for Word docs. Antiword is better for converting Word docs en masse.

PDF generation goes through LaTeX, which can't produce tagged (accessible) PDFs. Workaround: use Pandoc to convert to ODT, then run 'unoconv -f pdf -e UseTaggedPDF=true'. The user tried it and it works.
Converts Word docs into Markdown so they can be diffed like source code. Says it works great for legal redlining.

Tried to build invoices as CSV to Markdown tables to PDF, but couldn't get a second taxes table to align; cells went 'all over the place' with no info online. Gave up and still does invoices manually in LibreOffice Writer.
Every couple of years they relearn the same idiosyncrasies: odd defaults, annoying depths to customize HTML templates, and a weird filter infrastructure.
Typeset their novel with Pandoc. The editor and publisher were impressed by how clean the output was, and in the end the publisher used Pandoc's PDFs instead of InDesign.
Found many edge cases where Pandoc doesn't parse Org-mode properly. Sometimes even simple things like internal links aren't rendered correctly in the output.
If you find a bug, the maintainer will fix it within hours of your GitHub report.

On a modeling project, scripts wrote model inputs as Markdown tables embedded in a Markdown writeup, and Pandoc produced the Word report for sponsors. Without that automation they couldn't have trusted that all the tabular data was right.
Ubuntu apt installation is horrible: 'sudo apt install pandoc' forces a massive system-level TeX Live install even though they already have TeX Live in their home directory.
Falls short of a Swiss army knife: there are many conversions it can't do, like PDF-to-anything. Calibre's ebook-convert covers many of Pandoc's blind spots.
Writing their PhD thesis in Markdown, using filters like pandoc-plot and pandoc-crossref to transform documents mid-conversion and augment what Markdown can do.
Of every Markdown-to-docx tool they've tried, Pandoc is the only one that consistently maps Markdown headers to real Word styles rather than just bigger fonts.
Complains that it automatically converts straight quotes into 'smart' quotes by default, mangling any code that depends on quotes. Calls it the most awful default setting they've seen in a while.

Annoyed that in 3.0 the 'pandoc' package no longer provides the 'pandoc' executable, which breaks existing scripts. Otherwise loves the Lua filters for generating blog posts with a real programming language.

Could never get PDF generation working nicely: tables broke with overlapping text, Unicode fallback silently dropped characters like '→', and page breaks couldn't be controlled. Found wrestling with Markdown, LaTeX templates and config unintuitive, and went back to Word.

For docx output, the reference doc supplies only styles, so inserting a title page isn't straightforward. Workarounds: merging a Word title page with the DocxMerge tool, and a PowerShell script to autofit tables that don't fit contents properly.
